inventory.visualPurpose: The 'Ingested seafood toxins' table (book 246, top): three seafood toxin rows — histamine/scombroid, tetrodotoxin, ciguatoxin — with their sources, actions, symptoms, and treatments
inventory.sourceFigureDescription: COLOR-CODED TABLE, no raster (pdfimages: zero raster images; VLM-read at 120dpi, staging-ph21/vlm-census.txt — VLM available this session): one introductory sentence (initial letters h/t/c printed in red — First Aid's own mnemonic), then a five-column table (TOXIN / SOURCE / ACTION / SYMPTOMS / TREATMENT) with three rows in printed order — [1] Histamine (scombroid poisoning; toxin name teal with red first letter H): spoiled dark-meat fish such as tuna, mahi-mahi, mackerel, and bonito; bacterial histidine decarboxylase converts histidine to histamine, with 'Frequently misdiagnosed as fish allergy' printed INSIDE the ACTION cell; mimics anaphylaxis: oral burning sensation, facial flushing, erythema, urticaria, itching; may progress to bronchospasm, angioedema, hypotension; antihistamines, albuterol +/– epinephrine; [2] Tetrodotoxin (red first letter T): pufferfish; binds fast voltage-gated Na+ channels in nerve tissue, preventing depolarization; nausea, diarrhea, paresthesias, weakness, dizziness, loss of reflexes; supportive; [3] Ciguatoxin (red first letter C): reef fish such as barracuda, snapper, and moray eel; opens Na+ channels, causing depolarization; nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, perioral numbness, reversal of hot and cold sensations, bradycardia, heart block, hypotension; supportive. NO shellfish/saxitoxin row prints (VLM-confirmed). Light-blue shading on the TOXIN column; no figures, icons, or margin notes.

inventory.visualPurpose: The 'Plant toxins' table (book 246, bottom): five plant toxin rows — grayanotoxin, aconitine, cardiac glycosides, coniine, atropine/scopolamine — with their sources, actions, symptoms, and treatments
inventory.sourceFigureDescription: COLOR-CODED TABLE, no raster (pdfimages: zero raster images; VLM-read at 120dpi, staging-ph21/vlm-census.txt — VLM available this session): the five-column header row (TOXIN / SOURCE / ACTION / SYMPTOMS / TREATMENT) repeats over this table, which carries five rows in printed order — [1] Grayanotoxin: Rhododendron nectar ('mad honey'); opens voltage-gated Na+ channels → prolonged depolarization → ↑ vagal tone; nausea, vomiting, dizziness, bradycardia, hypotension; supportive care (IV fluids, atropine if severe bradycardia); [2] Aconitine alkaloids: Aconitum (monkshood, wolfsbane); activates Na+ channels (site 2) → delayed inactivation → sustained Na+ influx → ventricular arrhythmias; paresthesias, hypotension, ventricular tachyarrhythmias, cardiac arrest; supportive, lidocaine or amiodarone for arrhythmia; avoid class IA/III agents; [3] Cardiac glycosides: Digitalis purpurea, Nerium oleander; inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase → ↑ intracellular Na+ → ↑ Na+/Ca²+ exchanger → ↑ Ca²+ → ↑ vagal tone, ectopy; GI upset, visual disturbances (xanthopsia), AV block, arrhythmias; digoxin-specific Fab, atropine for bradycardia, correct K+/Mg²+; [4] Coniine (hemlock): Conium maculatum (poison hemlock); nicotinic ACh receptor agonist/antagonist → depolarizing blockade → flaccid paralysis; ascending paralysis, respiratory failure, salivation; supportive (respiratory support); activated charcoal early; [5] Atropine/scopolamine: Atropa belladonna, Datura stramonium ('jimsonweed'); muscarinic ACh receptor antagonist; anticholinergic toxidrome: dry mouth, mydriasis, hyperthermia, delirium; physostigmine (AChE inhibitor), cooling, fluids. NO ricin / cyanogenic / water-hemlock rows print (VLM-confirmed). Light-blue shading on the TOXIN column; species names in italics; no figures, icons, or margin notes.
